clinical_category: Cerebral perfusion pressure - calculation from MAP and ICP
blueprint_topic: Interpretation of hemodynamic and intracranial monitoring data
stem: A client has a mean arterial pressure of 90 mm Hg and an intracranial pressure of 20 mm Hg measured at the same time. What is the client's cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)?
rationale: A is correct. Cerebral perfusion pressure is calculated as mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure: CPP = MAP − ICP. With MAP 90 mm Hg and ICP 20 mm Hg, CPP is 70 mm Hg. CPP represents the net pressure gradient supporting cerebral perfusion; when MAP is unchanged, an increase in ICP lowers CPP. B incorrectly adds MAP and ICP. C reports MAP alone. D reports ICP alone. The item deliberately tests the verified calculation and physiologic relationship without assigning a universal treatment target to every neurologic condition.
educational_objective: Calculate cerebral perfusion pressure using CPP = MAP − ICP and recognize that rising intracranial pressure can reduce the pressure gradient supporting cerebral blood flow when systemic pressure is unchanged.
source_document_title: Cerebral Perfusion Pressure; Physiology, Cerebral Autoregulation
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf 'Cerebral Perfusion Pressure' → Definition/Introduction: CPP is the net pressure gradient that drives oxygen delivery to cerebral tissue and is the difference between MAP and ICP; CPP = MAP − ICP. NCBI Bookshelf 'Physiology, Cerebral Autoregulation' → cerebral blood flow depends on CPP and cerebrovascular resistance; CPP represents the pressure gradient between arterial pressure and the cerebral venous/intracranial pressure compartment.
source_claim_supported: Current NCBI/StatPearls content directly supports the CPP = MAP − ICP calculation and the interpretation of CPP as the pressure gradient supporting cerebral perfusion.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential client-needs subcategory (9–15% of items); this item tests calculation and interpretation of monitoring data used to identify neurologic perfusion risk.
correction_summary: Substantive refinement. The original generic AANN item asked only what CPP conceptually represents. The final item uses a directly supported formula in a concrete bedside calculation and avoids adding a condition-independent CPP treatment target.
audit_findings: The original generic AANN source failed the exact-locator requirement.
Current StatPearls directly defines CPP as MAP minus ICP and as the net cerebral perfusion pressure gradient.
All numeric values in the item are used only in the directly supported formula; no unverified therapeutic target or intervention threshold is introduced.
Distractors represent common calculation errors—sum, MAP alone, or ICP alone—and none is clinically defensible as CPP.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct calculation, no second defensible option, no unsupported precision, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
